R001.Description: Fungal disease attacking leaves, fruit and wood. It overwinters in mummified fruit and cankered wood, then releases spores during warm rain events. Frog-eye leaf spots are the visible stage; the economic damage comes from fruit rot and limb cankers that girdle branches over successive seasons.
Symptoms: Circular 'frog-eye' leaf spots: purple margin, tan centre
Firm brown fruit rot with concentric rings, often starting at the calyx
Sunken reddish-brown cankers on limbs, bark peeling at the edges
Mummified fruit persisting on the tree through winter
Treatment_Chemical: Captan 80 WG at 1.9 kg/ha from pink bud, repeat every 10-14 days in wet weather
Thiophanate-methyl 70 WP (FRAC 1) at petal fall — alternate to avoid resistance
Difenoconazole (FRAC 3) during fruit development, max 3 applications per season
Treatment_Biological: Bacillus subtilis QST 713 sprays every 7 days as a preventive rotation partner
Trichoderma harzianum paste on pruning wounds to block canker colonisation
Treatment_Organic: Copper hydroxide at silver tip / green tip (dormant to early bud)
Lime sulphur dormant spray to reduce overwintering inoculum
Remove and burn all mummified fruit and cankered wood in winter
Irrigation: Switch to drip or under-tree micro-sprinklers — never wet the canopy
Irrigate early morning so foliage dries before nightfall
Avoid over-irrigation during ripening: soft fruit is far more infectible
Fertilization: Balanced NPK; keep nitrogen moderate — lush growth is highly susceptible
Calcium sprays (calcium chloride 0.5%) during fruit sizing to firm the skin
Apply potassium in late season to harden wood before dormancy
Pruning: Cut cankered limbs 20-30 cm below the visible margin, in dry weather
Disinfect secateurs with 70% alcohol between every cut
Open the canopy for airflow; destroy all prunings off-site — do not compost
Monitoring: Inspect fruit clusters and limb crotches after every rain event
Flag and map cankered limbs for winter removal
Prevention: Sanitation is the single highest-return action: remove mummies and deadwood
Avoid mechanical wounds; protect large cuts with wound sealant
Maintain vigour — stressed and winter-injured trees are colonised first
Crop_Management: Sanitation is the single highest-return action: remove mummies and deadwood
Avoid mechanical wounds; protect large cuts with wound sealant
R001.Recovery_Time: Leaf infections stop in 2-3 weeks with control; wood cankers require 1-2 seasons of sanitation
Warnings: Fruit already showing rot cannot be cured — remove it to stop spore production

R003.Description: A rust requiring two hosts: juniper/cedar and apple. Galls on nearby junipers swell after spring rain and release spores that infect apple leaves. Without a juniper within roughly 1-2 km the disease cannot complete its cycle, which makes host removal the most durable control.
Symptoms: Bright yellow-orange spots on the upper leaf surface, often with a red border
Tube-like fringed structures (aecia) on the underside of the spots
Premature defoliation in heavy years; deformed, spotted fruit
Orange gelatinous galls on nearby juniper after spring rain
Treatment_Chemical: Myclobutanil (FRAC 3) from pink bud, repeating at 10-day intervals through spore release
Difenoconazole or tebuconazole as alternates within the same window
Mancozeb 80 WP as a protectant partner early in the season
Treatment_Biological: Bacillus subtilis as a low-pressure preventive; limited curative effect on rust
Treatment_Organic: Sulphur sprays applied preventively before infection periods
Remove juniper galls in late winter within 1 km where feasible
Plant resistant cultivars (e.g. Liberty, Freedom, Enterprise) on replanting
Irrigation: Drip irrigation only — spore germination requires 4-6 h of leaf wetness
No overhead watering between green tip and 3 weeks after petal fall
Fertilization: Standard balanced programme; support defoliated trees with a light foliar feed
Avoid heavy late nitrogen which prolongs susceptible young growth
Pruning: Thin the canopy so leaves dry quickly after rain
No specific rust pruning needed — the fungus does not form cankers on apple
Monitoring: Watch junipers after the first warm spring rains — orange horns mean spores are flying
Scout apple leaves 10-14 days after each release event
Prevention: Break the two-host cycle: remove or replace nearby junipers/cedars
Time all sprays to the spring gall-release window; sprays after that are wasted
Choose resistant rootstock-cultivar combinations for new plantings
Crop_Management: Break the two-host cycle: remove or replace nearby junipers/cedars
Time all sprays to the spring gall-release window; sprays after that are wasted

Warnings: Sprays applied after the juniper gall window give no benefit — timing is everything

R007.Description: The most economically damaging apple disease in humid climates. Ascospores are discharged from overwintered leaf litter during spring rain; infection depends on the combination of temperature and hours of leaf wetness described by the Mills table. Left uncontrolled it causes total fruit downgrade.
Symptoms: Olive-green velvety lesions on leaves, later turning dark and corky
Leaf puckering and distortion around lesions; early defoliation
Rough scabby corky patches on fruit, sometimes cracking
Lesions on the underside of sepals in early season
Treatment_Chemical: Protectant: mancozeb or captan applied before each predicted infection period
Curative (within 72 h of infection): difenoconazole or myclobutanil (FRAC 3)
Post-infection: dodine or an SDHI (FRAC 7) — strictly alternate FRAC groups
Treatment_Biological: Bacillus subtilis QST 713 in low-pressure periods and close to harvest
Autumn urea spray on leaf litter (5%) to accelerate microbial breakdown of inoculum
Treatment_Organic: Sulphur or copper on a strict 7-day preventive schedule in the primary season
Shred and remove fallen leaves in autumn — the primary inoculum source
Grow scab-resistant (Vf gene) cultivars where replanting
Irrigation: Eliminate overhead irrigation entirely during the primary infection season
Irrigate at dawn so any wetting period is as short as possible
Fertilization: Moderate nitrogen — succulent shoots stay susceptible longer
Autumn urea application doubles as sanitation and nutrition
Support defoliated trees with potassium to protect next year's bud set
Pruning: Winter-prune for an open canopy: faster drying is direct disease control
Remove watersprouts which form dense, humid interior growth
Monitoring: Track leaf wetness hours and temperature to identify infection periods
Scout terminal leaves and fruitlets 10-14 days after each wet event
Prevention: Autumn leaf-litter removal cuts primary inoculum dramatically
Use a Mills-table or weather-station model to time sprays rather than the calendar
Maintain protectant cover on all new growth during rainy spells
Crop_Management: Autumn leaf-litter removal cuts primary inoculum dramatically
Use a Mills-table or weather-station model to time sprays rather than the calendar
R007.Recovery_Time: New infection halts within 1-2 weeks of correct spraying; existing fruit scabs are permanent
Warnings: Scabbed fruit cannot be cured — the goal is protecting uninfected tissue
V. inaequalis develops resistance quickly: never apply the same FRAC group twice in a row
Respect pre-harvest intervals; scab sprays often run late into the season
References: FAO Plant Production and Protection guidelines
